title: 2013_PMC4515582_Are_Recent_Medical_Graduates_More_Skeptical_of_Vaccines
ehr_evidence: Surveys covering vaccine knowledge, attitudes, and beliefs were mailed in 2005 to 712 of these parent-identified providers.
summary: A cross-sectional survey study conducted in 2005 of 551 U.S. primary care providers examining the association of provider year of graduation with beliefs about vaccine efficacy, vaccine safety, disease susceptibility, and disease severity.
key_findings: More recent graduates had 15% decreased odds of believing vaccines are efficacious compared to the preceding 5-year interval (OR: 0.85, 95% CI: 0.73–0.99).
For every 5-year increase in graduation year there was 24% reduced odds of believing immunizations are one of the safest forms of medicine ever developed (OR: 0.76, 95% CI: 0.67–0.87).
Recent graduates had 1.4 times higher odds of believing immunizations do more harm than good compared to older providers.
There was a statistically significant 10% increased odds that more recent graduates believe vaccines strengthen the immune system.
Provider belief in disease susceptibility was not associated with graduation year (OR: 0.94, 95% CI: 0.78–1.13) and disease severity showed no association (OR: 1.05, 95% CI: 0.95–1.17).
3.7% of recent graduates believed immunizations do more harm than good.
captured_features: Provider type (MD, DO, ND, NP, RN)
population: 551 U.S. primary care providers (86% MD) identified by parents of fully vaccinated or school-immunization-exempt children in Colorado, Massachusetts, Missouri, and Washington; surveyed in 2005.
exposure_domain: Vaccine attitudes/beliefs and provider graduation cohort (age proxy)
limitations: Provider survey nested in a case-control design, so providers were not representative of all U.S. health care providers.
Graduation year used as a proxy for age rather than precise age.
Insufficient sample size for some non-significant findings.
Data collected in 2005, so associations may have changed for younger providers.
